flashcards.q: How many patch tokens does a 224x224 image with 16x16 patches produce for a ViT, including the CLS token?
flashcards.a: (224/16)^2 = 196 patches, plus 1 learned [CLS] token = 197 total sequence positions entering the transformer encoder.

flashcards.q: Why does a Vision Transformer need an explicit positional embedding when a CNN doesn't?
flashcards.a: Self-attention is permutation-invariant with no inherent sense of spatial layout, unlike a CNN's convolution which is inherently local and translation-equivariant. A learned positional embedding is added elementwise to each patch embedding so the model knows patch order.

flashcards.q: Describe CLIP's contrastive training objective mechanically.
flashcards.a: For a batch of N (image, caption) pairs, build the NxN cosine-similarity matrix between L2-normalized image and text embeddings. Symmetric cross-entropy pushes the diagonal (true pairs) highest in both image-to-text and text-to-image directions; every off-diagonal pair is a free in-batch negative.

flashcards.q: Why does CLIP pretraining use a very large batch size (32,768 in the original paper)?
flashcards.a: Every other item in the batch serves as a negative example for every anchor pair -- a larger batch gives more and harder in-batch negatives per gradient step, directly shaping the embedding space's discriminative geometry.

flashcards.q: Is a 'vision token' the same kind of object as a text token inside an LLM's context?
flashcards.a: No -- a text token is a discrete id from a fixed vocabulary looked up in an embedding table. A vision token is a continuous vector from a vision encoder plus projection layer, with no vocabulary entry and no decode() back to a symbol. Self-attention treats both identically once in the sequence, but they can't be constrained-decoded or filtered by text guardrails.

flashcards.q: Roughly how many vision tokens does LLaVA-1.5 use per image, and is this count fixed or variable?
flashcards.a: Fixed at 576 tokens for a 336x336 image (24x24 patches at 14px), regardless of the image's actual size or visual complexity -- always the same count.

flashcards.q: What is GPT-4o's approximate token cost for a 1024x1024 image in high-detail mode, and what's the formula?
flashcards.a: Roughly 765 tokens: a flat 85-token base cost plus 170 tokens per 512x512 tile after scaling to fit within 2048x2048 then shortest side to 768px. Low-detail mode is a flat 85 tokens regardless of size.

flashcards.q: What's Claude's image token cost formula, and what does a 1000x1000 image cost?
flashcards.a: tokens = (width_px * height_px) / 750. A 1000x1000 image (1 megapixel) costs roughly 1,334 tokens; images are downscaled if the long edge exceeds the model's cap (1,568px in earlier Claude models, 2,576px in Opus 4.7).

flashcards.q: What does Qwen2.5-VL's 'Naive Dynamic Resolution' do differently from LLaVA's fixed-patch approach?
flashcards.a: The vision encoder processes images at native aspect ratio/resolution rather than forcing a fixed resize, and a merger module produces a variable vision-token count (roughly 4 to 16,384) proportional to actual visual content -- far more token-efficient, at the cost of more implementation complexity.

30-second audio chunks at 16kHz become an 80-bin (large-v2 and earlier) or 128-bin (large-v3+) log-mel spectrogram, 10ms hop. Two conv layers downsample, sinusoidal positional embeddings are added, then a transformer encoder processes it. An autoregressive BPE decoder cross-attends into encoder states to generate text tokens.

flashcards.q: Is Whisper's integration with an LLM the same kind of fusion as a VLM's vision-token fusion?
flashcards.a: No -- by default it's a cascaded pipeline: Whisper outputs discrete text tokens as a standalone ASR step, and that transcript is fed into the LLM as ordinary text. There's no shared embedding space the way a VLM projects continuous vision embeddings directly into the LLM's sequence.

flashcards.q: What is a CLIP typographic attack, and why does it work?
flashcards.a: Pasting text onto an image (e.g. the word 'iPod' written on a photo of an apple) can shift the embedding toward that word's semantic neighborhood strongly enough to flip zero-shot classification, because contrastive training never explicitly taught the model to distinguish depicted content from depicted text -- both correlate with caption text in the training distribution.
